Because the map f is not isomorphic (e.g., since M<N), it will not preserve the ratios of singlet and doublet distributions, i.e., in general ~PDðuÞ= ~PSðuÞsPDðfðuÞÞ=PSðfðuÞÞ. This means that a multiplet state u could appear embedded in one map U1, but neotypic in another map U2. This is easy to appreciate: for example, if analysis is restricted to one subset of genes, then some doublets may be neotypic, while restriction to another subset of genes might cause the same doublets to be embedded. The operational dependence of doublet classiﬁcation on the choice of map f means that the nature of doublet errors cannot be considered to be immutable properties of the doublets. Given that the data represent a similar number of cells from each individual, roughly 7 out of 8 doublets should occur between individuals and can be identiﬁed using this approach. Thus, in the ground truth data, we expect at least 12.5% of true doublets to be undetected.
